title: A Reproducible Quality-Assurance Benchmark for Detecting Contextual Carryover in Biomedical Long-Context AI Assistants
abstract: <jats:p>Background and Objective:Long-context large language model (LLM) assistants are increasingly used for biomedical research planning. A practical reliability risk is contextual carryover: obsolete entities or constraints from a previous task may contaminate a new experimental request after a deliberate topic switch. This study introduces a reproducible quality-assurance benchmark and analysis program for detecting contextual carryover in biomedical long-context AI assistants.Methods:The benchmark contains 1,600 matched synthetic biomedical task-switch prompts covering disease models, cell types, assays or omics modalities, candidate drugs, pathways, experimental goals, and safety or ethics constraints. The evaluation program combines sparse residual-stream diagnostics, risk-enriched stress testing, balanced non-enriched checks, same-backend counterfactual controls, direct-parent sensitivity analysis, auxiliary multi-model behavioral coverage, a deployment-oriented dry-run case study, and expert calibration. Two independent biomedical experts with more than ten years of domain experience annotated validation subsets, with adjudication by a senior experimental researcher with more than fifteen years of experience. Automated labels were produced by a fixed Qwen judge rubric and calibrated against expert labels.Results:Representation diagnostics showed that OpenBioLLM had stronger input-proximal old-entity anchoring but lower middle/late old-entity alignment and greater boundary separation than the general comparator. In same-backend counterfactual controls, OpenBioLLM showed a stronger original-A-specific obsolete-entity signal than Llama-3.1-70B (13.5% vs. 3.0%; Fisher&apos;s exact p = 0.000181). In a direct Llama-3 sensitivity subset (n = 382), aggregate semantic carryover was comparable between Llama-3 and OpenBioLLM (15.7% vs. 14.4%; paired difference -1.3 percentage points; bootstrap 95% CI -5.8 to 3.4; McNemar p = 0.653), but category-specific vulnerability differed. Balanced expert validation showed that the automated judge achieved 76.9% precision, 100.0% recall, 98.9% specificity, and 87.0% F1 against strict agreed human carryover labels. A 30-case deployment-oriented dry run showed no baseline carryover under the tested Llama-3.1 route (0/30) but detected one safety-context residue under a QA-intervention prompt (1/30), illustrating how the workflow can audit both assistant behavior and guardrail prompts before release.Conclusions:Contextual carryover is a measurable task-switching reliability risk in biomedical LLM assistants. The proposed benchmark is best interpreted as a reproducible quality-assurance program, regression test, and guardrail-prompt audit rather than a model leaderboard or a real-world prevalence estimator.</jats:p>

title: Forced Verdict Gates, Not Graph Sophistication: A Multi-Framework Benchmark of AI Audit Judgement on Real-World Scandal Cases
abstract:
<jats:p>We benchmark four multi-agent orchestration frameworks (plain-Python Blackboard, CrewAI, OpenAI Swarm, LangGraph) on a shared audit-judgement task: four AI agents embodying canonical audit personas (Engagement Partner, Audit Senior, Skeptic Reviewer, Independence Checker) must each form an audit opinion on four real-world corporate scandals (Enron 2001, Wirecard 2020, SVB 2023, Tesco 2014), using only the public information available before each scandal broke. Each framework's output is scored against hidden ground truth on four axesjudgement accuracy, evidence rigour (red-flag recall), reasoning quality (LLM-judged), and calibration-plus a manual framework-ergonomics axis.&nbsp;
<div>
 The lowest-abstraction framework (plain Python with a Blackboard pattern) outperformed the three production frameworks (15.33 vs 13.84, 12.94, 5.00 out of 20 on auto-scored axes). We initially hypothesised the differentiator was a forced verdict gate-an independence-checker node that rejects unsupported opinions and forces rework. A deconfounding experiment adding the gate to LangGraph did not confirm this: the gated variant (12.64-13.01) did not recover plain_python's score, ruling out the gate as the sole driver and leaving the Blackboard's input-digest reactivity as the leading alternative explanation. Evidence-surfacing and opinion-formation emerged as decoupled capabilities: the framework with the highest red-flag recall (Swarm, 4.44/5, including 100% on one case) had the lowest judgement accuracy (1.50/5) and refused to commit to any verdict. Agents were systematically over-cautious relative to the real auditors who failed (0 of 16 runs issued a "Clean" opinion; the real auditors issued Clean on all four), and mostly correctly so given the evidence constraint. The paper was independently peer-reviewed by a second LangGraph multi-agent system (three reviewer personas + editor, with a conditional reconsideration loop); the peer review correctly identified the gate-framework confound that the deconfounding experiment confirmed. We discuss implications for multi-agent framework design, LLM-as-auditor research, and the audit profession's structural under-caution problem.
</div></jats:p>

title: Lightweight Edge AI framework for Real Time Air Quality Analysis
abstract: Recent developments in the field of machine learning and deep learning have led to the improvement of air quality monitoring and forecasting, which allows making more accurate, efficient, and scalable predictions.Most of the current solutions are based on large models that require significant computing capabilities or continuous connectivity with a cloud, which limits their use in resource-constrained environments. The model presented in this paper is a lightweight Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) that was trained on one year of historical data (365 days) of the Open-Meteo API and then connected to low-cost IoT sensors (PMS7003 to measure PM2.5/PM10 and DHT22 to measure temperature/humidity) on a microcontroller (ESP32). With the help of TensorFlow Lite (TFLite) to infer the model on-the-fly, the model demonstrates high performance with an R2 of 0.9402, Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of 0.0367 and Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) of 0.0424 and has minimal resource needs in relation to the more traditional methods. The proposed system provides a high level of efficiency and edge deployment practicable than traditional benchmarks and is most appropriate to mobile platforms and resource constrained platforms. The study offers a convenient, practical system of real time air quality intelligence in emerging economies.

title: Before the Algorithm: The BRAIF AI Readiness Framework for Indian PSUs, MSMEs and Statutory InstitutionsA Suggested Benchmark Approach for Determining AI Readiness, and for Structuring Responsible AI Selection and Engagement
abstract:
<jats:p><div>
 <p>Indian public sector undertakings (PSUs), micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) and statutory institutions are under growing pressure to adopt artificial intelligence, yet most start from different positions and face different constraints. Many begin tools before they have decided what AI is for, who is accountable, where data may lawfully reside, how employees are already using unsanctioned tools, or what the whole programme will cost and return.&nbsp;&nbsp;<span>Others stall because the path to adoption is unclear.&nbsp;</span></p>
 <p>This paper proposes an AI Readiness Framework (BRAIF-AIR), a suggested benchmark approach for determining the AI readiness of these three organisational types and for turning the result into a pathway and a selection method. It comprises a Gate that profiles the organisation, and eleven readiness dimensions in four clusters (direction; assurance; foundations; capability and value), covering strategy and value, governance and policy, risk, legal compliance, data foundation, data residency and sovereignty, technology, security and shadow AI, people and culture, finance and return on investment, and ecosystem and procurement. The framework is operationalised through 87 indicators with entity-specific applicability, a five-level maturity scale tied to evidence, gating thresholds that apply a weakest-link rule rather than averaging, four readiness pathways, a use-case triage method, and an assessment protocol for consultants with integrity safeguards.&nbsp;</p>
 <p>A Responsible AI Audit Mechanism is integrated as the selection and engagement method that readiness unlocks, and the challenges identified are consolidated in a single register. The method combines a synthesis of readiness, maturity-model and public-sector AI literature with design-science construction; evaluation is proposed but not yet performed.&nbsp;</p>
 <p>The framework is deliberately not definitive: it is a nudge and a starting benchmark for researchers to test and extend and for consultants to adopt with care.</p>
</div>
<div>
 <br>
</div></jats:p>

title: Evidence Quality in Assurance-Oriented Benchmark Construction
abstract: Assurance studies built from public software incidents depend on evidence whose fitness for reconstruction and downstream assurance analysis is rarely characterized at the level of the semantic claims the analysis consumes. We study this evidence-quality problem in a frozen 40-case frame of public tool-using-agent and Model Context Protocol incidents, separating reconstructability, replay/source resolution, oracle feasibility, pairing, releaseability, and element-level provenance of authored assurance semantics. Reproducible-vulnerability benchmarks and vulnerability-data-quality studies already establish disclosure filtering and intrinsic data-quality assessment; our contribution is narrower and task-relative. Although 39/40 cases exposed a patch or corrected state, only 20/40 met the strict paired criteria. Among 15 prefix survivors that were not strict-eligible, nonexclusive blockers were reconstruction (14), releaseability (9), replay/source resolution (4), pairing (3), and oracle feasibility (1); C38 was technically reconstructable but excluded solely by Conditional releaseability. In a ten-case deep audit, 190 representation rows were provenance-classified, and all 52 analyzer-relevant semantic attributes were source-informed rather than independent ground truth. C4 showed conclusion-relevant uncertainty: unresolved enforcement activity produced different fixed-state conclusions under fail-open versus fail-closed assignments. We additionally release AIRR-40, a 40-case, 49-field registry with a 20-case exact-upstream strict manifest and reproducibility artifacts. The study does not estimate population readiness or detector accuracy; it characterizes evidence quality for assurance-oriented benchmark construction.

title: Review for "OPENXRD: A Comprehensive Benchmark Framework for LLM/MLLM XRD Question Answering"
Multi-Model Clinical Validation of an AI-Powered Biomarker Analysis Framework: A Cross-Vendor Benchmark on 4,018 NHANES Patients
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                <jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Large language models (LLMs) show promise for clinical decision support, yet most validation studies evaluate single models, leaving questions about generalizability and vendor dependence unanswered. We assessed whether a standardized biomarker analysis framework maintains clinical-grade accuracy across multiple LLMs from independent providers.</jats:p>
                </jats:sec>
                <jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>We developed a structured prompt-based framework for detecting eight clinical patterns (insulin resistance, diabetes, cardiovascular disease risk, chronic kidney disease risk, systemic inflammation, nutrient deficiency, liver risk, and anemia) from laboratory biomarkers. We evaluated five LLMs from four providers—Grok-3 (xAI), GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini (OpenAI), Claude Haiku 4.5 (Anthropic), and Gemini 2.0 Flash (Google)—using identical system prompts and inputs on 4,018 adults from the CDC NHANES 2017–2018. Ground truth was established using published clinical criteria (ADA, AHA, KDIGO, WHO). Performance was measured by F1 score with 95% confidence intervals, sensitivity, specificity, and positive predictive value.</jats:p>
                </jats:sec>
                <jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>All five models achieved clinical-grade performance (F1 > 0.86) on eight evaluable patterns. Mean F1 scores ranged from 0.865 (95% CI: 0.799–0.931) for GPT-4o-mini to 0.963 (95% CI: 0.930–0.996) for Grok-3. Flagship models significantly outperformed economy-tier models (mean F1: 0.940 vs 0.881; paired t-test p=0.004). Grok-3 achieved near-perfect scores on liver risk (F1=1.000), anemia (0.999), and nutrient deficiency (0.997). Cardiovascular disease risk was the most challenging pattern (F1 range: 0.853–0.885). JSON parse rates exceeded 99.9% for all models. Total benchmark cost was approximately $59 USD.</jats:p>
                </jats:sec>
                <jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>A standardized prompt-based framework achieves clinical-grade accuracy across five LLMs from four independent providers, demonstrating model-agnostic generalizability. These findings support the feasibility of vendor-independent clinical AI systems that can leverage multiple models without requiring framework revalidation.</jats:p>
                </jats:sec>

title: GameIQA-AI: A Multi-Dimensional Quality Assessment Benchmark for AI-Generated Game Images
AI-Powered Low-Code App Development: A Benchmark Review for 2025 Digital Transformation
abstract: <jats:p>The rapid proliferation of highly capable, multimodal large language models (LLMs) throughout 2024 and 2025 has created a pivotal inflection point for the global workforce. This paper examines the emergent paradigm of human-AI collaboration, moving beyond the narrative of job displacement to a more nuanced analysis of task augmentation and skill evolution. We investigate the real-world integration of advanced AI assistants across key professional sectors-including creative industries, software development, and scientific research-to identify patterns of adoption and their impact on productivity, innovation, and an individual's sense of professional agency. Through a synthesis of recent case studies and labor market data, this analysis highlights the critical need for new training frameworks and organizational strategies that foster co-creativity between humans and AI. The findings suggest that enterprises prioritizing "AI literacy" and the redesign of workflows to leverage machine-generated insights are gaining a significant competitive advantage. This paper concludes with forwardlooking recommendations for educators, policymakers, and business leaders on cultivating a resilient and adaptive workforce prepared for a future where professional success is defined by the ability to effectively partner with intelligent systems.</jats:p>

title: Explainable and Prescriptive AI for Cyber-Physical NVH Quality Control in Smart Manufacturing: A Critical Review and Research Framework
abstract: <jats:p>Artificial intelligence is increasingly used to predict noise, vibration, and harshness (NVH), detect faults, and identify quality deviations in rotating machinery and smart manufacturing. Yet high predictive accuracy does not answer the engineering questions required for process improvement: which manufacturing or geometric variable generated the response, whether the relationship is causal, what controllable setting should change, whether the change is physically and technologically feasible, and whether the intervention improves the measured product. This critical review integrates five evidence streams: direct gear and drivetrain NVH studies; explainable rotating-machinery diagnosis; explainable manufacturing-quality prediction; causal, counterfactual, and recourse methods; and digital-twin or closed-loop industrial control. The literature shows strong progress in feature attribution, saliency analysis, physics-informed representation, and interpretable fault-state estimation, but direct gear/NVH studies remain concentrated at prediction and explanation levels. To separate algorithmic sophistication from demonstrated engineering capability, we propose a cumulative Level 0–6 maturity framework spanning prediction, global explanation, local explanation, engineering root cause, actionable recommendation, physics-constrained prescription, and closed-loop validation. The framework supports comparison of studies and design of cyber-physical NVH quality-control systems that progress from explanation to traceable, feasible, and experimentally validated manufacturing action.</jats:p>

title: Scorecard of AI Benchmark Quality
OpenEMR-AI: An Open-Source Ambient AI Scribe Framework, Benchmark, and Blinded Physician Evaluation (Preprint)
abstract:
BACKGROUND

Ambient artificial intelligence (AI) scribes are being deployed at scale, with randomized trials demonstrating reductions in documentation time and burnout indicators. However, two gaps limit equitable adoption and rigorous validation. First, current deployments depend almost entirely on proprietary infrastructure, placing ambient documentation out of practical reach for federally qualified health centers (FQHCs), critical-access hospitals, and low- and middle-income country (LMIC) health systems. Second, automated evaluation of ambient-generated notes relies heavily on embedding-based similarity metrics whose agreement with clinician judgment on full clinical documentation has not been rigorously quantified.

 OBJECTIVE

To develop and release an open-source, vendor-independent ambient clinical documentation framework integrated with the open-source OpenEMR electronic health record (EHR) via SMART on FHIR (SoF), and to quantify divergence between widely used automated metrics and blinded physician judgment of full clinical documentation.

 METHODS

We deployed a multi-tenant serverless SMART-on-FHIR application that writes FHIR R4 resources back to OpenEMR. We benchmarked 13 ASR models on 335 conversational clinical recordings and 380 short-form utterances across four datasets, and seven open-weight LLMs for retrieval-augmented clinical note generation grounded on 1,000 disease-specific MIMIC-IV schemas. Four top-performing LLMs generated 160 summaries for 40 Fareez OSCE conversations paired with OpenEMR patient records. Three board-eligible physician fellows produced 480 blinded ratings on six PDQI-9/QNOTE dimensions. Inter-rater reliability used Gwet’s AC2 with ordinal weights. Model differences used Friedman tests with Bonferroni-corrected post-hoc Wilcoxon signed-rank tests; Kendall’s W was reported with 95% percentile-bootstrap confidence intervals from 10,000 conversation-block resamples.

 RESULTS

BERTScore F1 was virtually identical across the four clinician-evaluated models (0.800-0.803), yet clinician composite scores spanned 2.95-3.74 with significant model differences (p ≤ 0.002 for completeness, organization, conciseness, clinical utility, and overall quality). MedCAT UMLS-linked entity recall, but not embedding-based metrics, showed clinically meaningful separation that distinguished the medically tuned 4B model (composite 2.95) from the three larger general-purpose models (3.61-3.74). Voxtral Mini 3B led on institutional and Fareez OSCE recordings; medical-dictation ASR failed catastrophically. Per-encounter cost was approximately $0.02, a 98-99% reduction relative to commercial alternatives. Two persistent LLM failure modes of chart-overreach (≈22% of clinician comments, lower-bound estimate) and fabrication (≈21%) were intrinsic to current LLM behavior and require physician attestation.

 CONCLUSIONS

Embedding-based automated metrics systematically understate clinically meaningful quality differences that physicians detect in ambient-AI-generated notes; entity-based metrics partially recover these differences. Procurement, certification (FDA, CE), and post-market surveillance frameworks for ambient-AI scribes should require clinician-anchored and entity-based evaluation as primary endpoints, with embedding similarity reported only as supporting context. The complete SoF app, evaluation code, rater packets, and de-identified ratings are released open-source, lowering the access barrier for safety-net and resource-constrained settings.

title: Can AI Understand Mandarin Speech Prosody?  A Framework and Benchmark Showcase
EMSEIF Provides an Explainable AI Framework for Multi Stakeholder Curriculum Feedback and Quality Assurance in Higher Education
abstract: Higher education quality-assurance systems collect large volumes of curriculum feedback from students, teachers, alumni, parents and employers, yet the dominant institutional workflow still reduces these voices to descriptive percentages and post-hoc minutes. This study validates an Explainable Multi-Stakeholder Educational Intelligence Framework (EMSEIF) that converts real-world stakeholder feedback into aspect-level evidence, auditable recommendations and curriculum-improvement actions. The empirical setting is a 2023–24 structured curriculum feedback corpus from a participating higher education institution (HEI), represented by stakeholder forms, graphical analyses, action-taken letters and governance minutes. The system combines a curriculum aspect taxonomy, an educational knowledge graph, aspect-based sentiment analysis (ABSA), transformer-based multi-task classification, SHAP and Integrated Gradients explanations, subgroup fairness auditing and a human-in-the-loop (HITL) intervention engine. Validation uses stratified 5-fold cross-validation, ANOVA, Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, confidence intervals, effect sizes, error analysis and ablation studies. Across stakeholder roles, the institutional evidence shows high but uneven satisfaction. Aerospace Engineering reported an overall impression distribution of 5.5% poor, 10.3% fair, 35.6% good, 30.4% very good and 18.2% excellent, while ECE showed 2.27% poor, 6.58% fair, 24.04% good, 36.66% very good and 30.43% excellent. EMSEIF improves macro-F1 over all classical and single-task transformer baselines and maps recurring concerns about practical exposure, internships, employability, AI/ML, ICT skills, communication, value-added courses and industry interaction into governance-ready recommendations. The principal contribution is not another conceptual AI-in-education framework. EMSEIF is positioned as an empirical educational intelligence system joining multi-stakeholder feedback, explainable NLP, curriculum knowledge graphs, statistical validation, fairness governance and action tracking. The result is a reproducible, institutionally deployable closed loop that moves from stakeholder voice to curriculum revision and measured improvement.

title: Review for "Theoretical Physics Benchmark (TPBench) - a dataset and study of AI reasoning capabilities in theoretical physics"
Why Generative AI Triumphs: A Conceptual Framework for Prediction Quality in AI Systems
Physics beats diffusion: Agentic AI-driven virtual screening benchmark on a GPCR target
abstract: Virtual screening (VS) campaigns require expert decisions at every stage, from active compound curation and decoy generation to receptor preparation, docking engine selection, and statistical evaluation. I show that an autonomous large language model (LLM) coding agent (Claude Code, Anthropic) can design and execute a complete VS benchmark pipeline without human coding intervention that requires only high-level scientific direction. The agent curated 1,000 FPR2 (a GPCR receptor) actives from ChEMBL (pChEMBL ≥ 5), generated ca. 10,000 property-matched decoys, prepared ligand libraries using two protocols (naive defaults and expert-guided), configured and ran docking with two fundamentally different engines; 1) Uni-Dock (GPU-accelerated physics-based) and 2) DiffDock (diffusion-based machine learning). Then it performed full statistical evaluation including ROC AUC, BEDROC, enrichment factors, DeLong tests, and paired bootstrap confidence intervals. Uni-Dock achieved ROC AUC = 0.70–0.73 with significant discrimination (permutation p < 0.0001), while DiffDock confidence scores yielded near-random performance (AUC = 0.54–0.56; Cliff’s d = negligible), consistent with its known underrepresentation of GPCR targets in training data. Expert-guided protocols improved Uni-Dock AUC by +0.020 (DeLong p = 0.003; paired bootstrap p = 0.002). Single-ligand redocking confirmed Vina reproduces the crystal pose (RMSD 0.22–0.39 Å) whereas both Uni-Dock batch mode (5.2–5.7 Å) and DiffDock (23–29 Å) failed. All code, data, and the agent’s skill file are openly available. Scientific contribution: This is the first demonstration of an LLM coding agent autonomously constructing a reproducible VS benchmark from scratch. The resulting benchmark provides the first head-to-head comparison of Uni-Dock and DiffDock on a GPCR target that reveals that physics-based docking (AUC = 0.70–0.73) substantially outperforms diffusion-based ML docking (AUC = 0.54–0.56, near-random) for this underrepresented target class.

title: MSR88 ASSESSING AI AND ML TOOL PERFORMANCE IN SLRS: A TARGETED LITERATURE REVIEW AND PERFORMANCE BENCHMARK FRAMEWORK
Measuring the Quality of AI-Generated Clinical Notes: A Systematic Review and Experimental Benchmark of Evaluation Methods
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                <jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>High-quality clinical documentation is essential for safe, effective care, yet producing it is time consuming and error prone. Large language models (LLMs) can assist with note generation, but clinical adoption is determined by the resulting note quality. However current evaluation practices vary, and their clinical relevance is unclear. Drawing on a multidisciplinary perspective, we examined how quality is assessed and how those assessments align with clinical demands.</jats:p>
                </jats:sec>
                <jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>We systematically searched Ovid Medline and Scopus on 10 April 2025 for peer-reviewed studies that used LLMs in generating clinical notes and included an evaluation of the quality of the resulting text. The screening followed PRISMA and the protocol was preregistered in PROSPERO. Data on metrics, and outcomes were synthesised narratively. Based on these findings, we designed an experimental setup to test the most common evaluation metrics and an LLM-as-evaluator, included for its scalability across large test sets. The experiment used synthetic cases with targeted perturbations.</jats:p>
                </jats:sec>
                <jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Thirty-seven studies were included. The reporting was dominated by lexical overlap metrics, chiefly ROUGE and BLEU. Semantic similarity metrics, such as BERTScore and BLEURT, were less common. A human evaluation was frequent but heterogeneous, with criteria and methods defined using varying degrees of detail; the most common foci were correctness, fluency, and aspects of clinical acceptability. In our experimental setup, lexical overlap metrics detected deletions and modifications but penalised meaning-preserving paraphrases. Semantic metrics and LLM-as-evaluators were more tolerant of paraphrased perturbations, yet remained sensitive to relevant changes, with performance varying by model and language.</jats:p>
                </jats:sec>
                <jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Interpretation</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Current practice relies on lexical overlap metrics that are useful for cursory checks but insufficient as proxies for quality. We recommend a layered strategy that pairs semantic metrics with LLM-as-evaluator for scalability and includes targeted human adjudication. Broader, safety-focused validation across institutions and languages is needed before routine deployment.</jats:p>
                </jats:sec>
                <jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Funding</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Business Finland through the GenAID research project. Personal grants listed under Acknowledgments.</jats:p>
                </jats:sec>

HCCD-DS: A Reproducible Benchmark Dataset for Human--AI Decision Support Under Contextual Uncertainty
abstract: Decision support pipelines increasingly combine machine learning predictions with human judgment, yet most public benchmarks evaluate model outputs only and do not encode the interaction process that determines final decisions. This limits reproducible analysis of when human intervention improves or degrades system-level performance.We introduce HCCD-DS, a reproducible benchmark dataset that models decision-time interaction between an AI recommender and users with different expertise levels under contextual uncertainty. Each decision instance links input context, system confidence, explainability metadata, human acceptance/override behavior, override rationale, and realized outcome. The dataset covers healthcare, cybersecurity, and Internet of Things (IoT) scenarios to support cross-domain evaluation.Empirical analyses and benchmark experiments show that human intervention is condition-dependent: expert overrides are more likely to improve outcomes, while novice overrides more often reduce success. In addition, human action variables are substantially more predictable than final outcomes, indicating a plausible gap between behavioral predictability and outcome uncertainty. By exposing this structure in a unified and reusable resource, HCCD-DS supports method development for human-aware decision support, trust calibration, and explanation-aware interaction policies.

title: Benchmark Evaluation of the WordBinary AI-Text Detection Model on 9,000 AI-Generated Texts and 2,000 Pre-2015 Human Academic-Paper Samples
abstract: The growing use of large language models has increased demand for systems capable of distinguishing AI-generated text from genuine human writing. Such systems must achieve high sensitivity to machine-generated content while maintaining a sufficiently low false-positive rate to protect human authors. This study evaluated the WordBinary AI-text detection model using 11,000 labelled text samples: 9,000 AI-generated samples and 2,000 samples obtained from pre-2015 human academic papers. The AI corpus included normal and humanised outputs associated with Claude, Cohere, DeepSeek, Gemini, Mistral, OpenAI and OpenRouter platform groups. The human corpus contained 400 samples from each of five academic disciplines: computer science, economics, statistics, physics and mathematics. The model classified all 9,000 AI-generated samples as AI and all 2,000 human academic samples as human. The resulting confusion matrix contained 9,000 true positives, 2,000 true negatives, no false negatives and no false positives. Observed sensitivity, specificity, precision, negative predictive value, F1 score, balanced accuracy and overall accuracy were therefore all 100%. Exact 95% binomial confidence intervals were 99.959% to 100% for sensitivity, 99.816% to 100% for specificity and 99.966% to 100% for overall accuracy. The one-sided implication of observing no false positives in 2,000 human samples is that the 95% upper confidence bound for the underlying false-positive rate is approximately 0.184%, subject to the assumption that observations were statistically independent. Platform-level mean AI scores ranged from 98.56% for DeepSeek-associated outputs to 99.98% for OpenAI-associated outputs. All normal and humanised AI groups achieved 100% observed recall. The highest AI score among the human academic samples was 1.07%, while approximate domain-level mean scores ranged from 0.01% to 0.31%. The results demonstrate complete classification of the supplied test set. They do not, however, establish universal 100% accuracy. Independent external validation, documentation of the decision threshold, control for training-test contamination, clustered statistical analysis, multilingual testing and evaluation on mixed-authorship and AI-polished documents are required before broader generalisation.

title: RNA3D-Decoy: A Large-Scale Benchmark Dataset of AI-Generated RNA Structure Models for Quality Assessment
abstract:
<jats:p>
                  Recent advances in AI-based RNA structure prediction have increased the availability of candidate models, but their accuracy remains variable. Developing reliable quality assessment (QA) methods requires datasets that represent contemporary prediction errors across diverse targets and molecular contexts. Here, we present RNA3D-Decoy, a large-scale bench-mark dataset comprising 103,549 decoys for 677 experimentally determined targets, including 416 RNA-only structures, 117 RNA structures with metal ions, and 144 RNA-protein complexes. Decoys were generated using five biomolecular predictors: AlphaFold 3, ESMFold2, Protenix, Chai-1, and Boltz-2. Each decoy is evaluated against its experimental reference using TM-score, lDDT, and RMSD, with global and local quality annotations where applicable. DockQ scores additionally characterize RNA-protein interface quality. Target grouping incorporates both RNA and protein sequence relationships to support dataset partitioning. Analyses reveal distinct quality distributions across dataset levels and target-dependent differences among predictors, with each predictor contributing the highest-TM-score model for a subset of targets. Broad pooled score distributions also coexist with limited within-target score variation, particularly for RNA-protein complexes, emphasizing the importance of target-level characterization. By combining AI-generated decoys, standardized quality labels, and structured metadata, RNA3D-Decoy provides a resource for developing and evaluating methods for global quality estimation, local error prediction, and candidate-model ranking. The dataset and accompanying code are available at:

title: A Dual-Branch Explainable AI Framework Combining Machine and Deep Learning for Air Quality Forecasting in Indian Cities
abstract: A precise Air Quality Index (AQI) forecasting is essential for ecosystem monitoring and societal health management. This study proposes a dual-branch explainable AI framework that brings together machine learning models (XGBoost, LightGBM,CatBoost, Linear Regression) and deep learning models (LSTM, GRU, TCN, Transformer) for AQI prediction across major Indian cities. Comprehensive preprocessing, including temporal feature extraction and rolling mean engineering, was applied to ensure high-quality and reliable inputs. The GRU model achieved the best performance with an R2 score of 0.9886 and an RMSE of 0.0032. A multi-level XAI analysis was incorporated, using Feature Importance for machine learning models and Integrated Gradients, Perturbation Sensitivity, Feature Occlusion, and Temporal Receptive Field Profiling for deep learning models. The results consistently identified AQI_7d_avg and AQI_30d_avg as the most influential predictors. The proposed framework combines strong predictive accuracy with transparent interpretability, supporting data-driven environmental policymaking and sustainable air pollution control system across Indian cities.

title: ProSocial AI as a Catalyst of Quality of Life: A Multilevel Framework for Pro-People, Pro-Planet, and Pro-Potential Futures
abstract: Artificial intelligence increasingly mediates how people learn, work, seek care, form relationships, access public services, and respond to environmental risk. Its quality-of-life effects extend beyond technical performance and economic productivity. This conceptual article develops the ProSocial AI-Quality of Life Catalyst Model (PAI-QOL), a multilevel framework explaining when and how AI can contribute to futures that are pro-people, pro-planet, and pro-potential. ProSocial AI is defined as AI deliberately designed, deployed, and governed to generate demonstrable and fairly distributed gains in multidimensional quality of life, strengthen human and collective capabilities, and protect the ecological conditions of future well-being. A problem-driven integrative synthesis identifies four conversion pathways: agency and capability, relational and social-capital, institutional and public-value, and regenerative and intergenerational. Their benefits depend on four enabling conditions: Double Literacy, meaningful participation, contestability, and proportionality. The model connects the 4T architecture of tailored, trained, tested, and targeted AI with a 4 x 4 lens spanning aspirations, emotions, thoughts, and sensations across individual, community and institutional, national and systemic, and planetary and intergenerational levels. Four propositions translate the framework into testable claims. A multidimensional measurement strategy distinguishes genuine prosocial contribution from intention, compliance, or branding. ProSocial AI emerges as a disciplined direction for innovation that expands agency, reinforces trustworthy relationships and institutions, preserves future capability, and produces social value within planetary limits.

title: A Benchmark Framework for Trajectory Vectorization in Unsupervised Settings
abstract: The growth of location-tracking technologies has generated large spatiotemporal datasets that require efficient analysis methods. Recent approaches focus on vectorizing the data as a preprocessing step to enable the application of off-the-shelf classical machine learning techniques. To date, such approaches have primarily been evaluated in supervised tasks. This paper presents a benchmark framework for assessing these methods in unsupervised settings, where no target labels are available. We extend and systematically evaluate five families of vectorization techniques: feature-based, shapelet-based, dictionary-based, matrix-based, and deep-learning-based, on a suite of synthetic and real-world datasets. The framework assesses both clustering quality and cross-vectorization diversity through quantitative and qualitative analyses. Overall, the findings demonstrate that these vectorization approaches offer a valuable option for unsupervised trajectory analysis. Additionally, our paper provides insight into which vectorization technique is most suitable for the specific characteristics of the task under analysis. For example, our findings indicate that feature-based approaches are most effective for capturing motion dynamics, while shapelet-based methods excel at identifying localized geometric patterns.

title: QNLP-Bench: A Standardized Benchmark and Evaluation Framework for Quantum Natural Language Processing
abstract: Quantum Natural Language Processing (QNLP) seeks to combine com positional models of meaning with quantum and quantum-inspired computational frameworks. While recent work has demonstrated the feasibility of implement ing such models, empirical results remain difficult to compare due to heteroge neous evaluation practices, weak or mismatched baselines, and limited reporting of computational resources. As a result, it is often unclear when compositional or quantum-inspired approaches are genuinely warranted. In this work, we introduce QNLP-Bench, a standardized benchmark and evalu ation framework designed to enable fair, reproducible, and compute-aware assess ment of QNLP models. The benchmark defines shared task specifications, fixed preprocessing pipelines, capacity-matched classical baselines, and explicit resource reporting requirements across classical, quantum-inspired, and quantum models. Rather than targeting claims of quantum advantage, QNLP-Bench aims to clar ify the empirical conditions under which compositional structure contributes to improved generalization. We provide a minimal but diagnostic experimental instantiation of the bench mark using controlled sentence classification tasks that separate lexically driven and role-sensitive regimes. The results demonstrate that simple baselines suffice on lexically separable tasks, while explicit encoding of grammatical structure is nec essary for success on role-dependent problems, albeit at increased computational cost. These findings illustrate the value of standardized, diagnostic benchmarks for grounding progress in QNLP and for guiding future research toward transparent and principled evaluation practices

title: From Data Quality to AI-Native Operating Models: A Practitioner Framework for Enterprise AI Capability Coherence
abstract: <jats:p>Enterprise artificial intelligence is often seen in the context of the capability of the models used, data availability, technology infrastructure, or responsible AI governance. But organizations might have all these things but still face challenges in scaling their AI in the business processes. The argument presented in this paper is that the problem is both organizational and technical. The success of enterprise AI requires a coherent set of capabilities covering data quality, data governance, data products, data contracts, AI platform, accountability, lineage, explainability, ownership, value measurement, and operating model. The main proposition developed in this paper is that capability coherence is essential for scaling enterprise AI. The paper explores the proposition via conceptual synthesis of 12 practitioner essays published between July and September 2026 on the topics including data quality and governance, data products, AI ecosystems, responsible AI, decision traceability, data ownership, governance value, and AI-native operating models. The practitioner corpus is considered together with existing research and institutional literature, including BCBS 239, NIST AI Risk Management Framework, data-mesh research, IT governance, and dynamic capabilities theory.</jats:p>

title: VQD-CTS Prediction Model: An AI-Driven Framework for Predicting Cost-to-Serve Using Engineering Velocity, Quality, and Developer Experience
abstract: Modern software engineering organizations leverage multi-dimensional perfor mance indicators—Velocity, Quality, and Developer Experience (DX)—to gauge delivery health. However, establishing a quantifiable link between these engineer ing signals and financial outcomes like Cost-to-Serve (CTS) remains a significant challenge. This paper proposes the VQD-CTS Prediction Model, a comprehensive machine learning framework designed to predict CTS using a synthesis of V-Q-D metrics. Our ensemble regression model, trained on extensive synthetic enter prise data, achieved an R2 score of 0.885 with MAE of 79.93. Feature importance analysis identified code complexity, defect density, cycle time, and infrastructure cost share as dominant predictors. This framework supports organizations a scal able, data-driven approach to forecast budgetary needs and optimize engineering investments.

title: A Biomedical Benchmark and Modular RAG Framework for Text2Cypher
abstract: Background Biomedical Knowledge Graphs (bioKGs) are increasingly used to integrate heterogeneous biomedical data, including genomic interactions, disease associations, and drug–target relationships. Property graph databases, such as Neo4j, provide an effective framework for representing and querying these data through the Cypher query language. However, writing Cypher queries requires substantial technical expertise, limiting the accessibility of bioKGs to domain experts. Although Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently shown promise for translating natural language (NL) questions into Cypher queries, progress in the biomedical domain remains constrained by the limited availability of representative benchmarks and reproducible evaluation frameworks. Results We present bio2C, a FAIR-compliant biomedical benchmark comprising 2,500 curated NL-Cypher pairs covering diverse biomedical information needs, graph schemas, and progressively more expressive Cypher constructs. Building upon this resource, we introduce a modular Retrieval-Augmented Generation framework that systematically combines graph schema descriptions, retrieved NL-Cypher examples, and query execution outputs, thereby establishing reproducible baselines for future Text2Cypher research. We evaluate the resulting pipelines using both proprietary (GPT) and open-source (LLaMA) LLMs together with their fine-tuned counterparts. Experimental results show that retrieving representative NL-Cypher examples consistently outperforms schema-based prompting, with particularly pronounced improvements for fine-tuned models. The best-performing configuration improves execution accuracy by 31.6 percentage points over current schema-based prompting strategies. Conclusions This work provides two complementary resources for biomed-ical Text2Cypher research: a high-quality FAIR benchmark and a modular evaluation framework for systematically studying retrieval-augmented prompting strategies. Together, they establish reproducible baselines for developing and comparing future Text2Cypher systems while demonstrating that carefully curated benchmarks and representative retrieval examples substantially improve Cypher generation over bioKGs. The benchmark, source code, and evaluated pipelines are publicly available through Zenodo and GitHub.

title: Reliability and construct validity of a multi-model LLM-as-judge evaluator battery for clinician-facing clinical question answering: a controlled adversarial benchmark study (Preprint)
abstract:
BACKGROUND

Open-ended clinical question systems generate fluent free-text for which conventional accuracy metrics are insufficient. Complex questions may admit more than one defensible answer depending on clinical context, jurisdiction, guideline version and the intent of the person asking. Human expert review remains important but is costly, hard to scale and variable. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as automated evaluators, but an LLM-as-judge should be characterised as a measurement instrument before its outputs are treated as evidence.

 OBJECTIVE

To characterise the inter-judge reliability, within-judge stability, severity-rating heterogeneity, difficulty discrimination and construct validity of an LLM-as-judge battery used to evaluate clinician-facing clinical question answering.

 METHODS

We evaluated a three-model FACTFULNESS ensemble (Claude Opus 4.7, Gemini 3.1 Pro, GPT-5.4, each with native web search) and a single-model COMPLETENESS evaluator (GPT-5.4) on an author-constructed adversarial bank of 1,424 clinical questions across five difficulty tiers and 16 construct families. Of 1,421 scored items, 1,173 (82.5%) carried complete three-judge verdicts. Agreement on binary factuality used Gwet AC1, Fleiss kappa and unanimity, overall and within 22 strata. Sensitivity analyses addressed the complete-case restriction, claim-set non-identity, repeated scoring and retrieved-evidence overlap.

 RESULTS

Gwet AC1 was 0.344 (95% CI 0.302-0.386), Fleiss kappa 0.212, and 46.3% of items unanimous. AC1 fell from 0.60 at difficulty tier D1 to 0.27 at D5, ranged from 0.79 to 0.13 across construct families, and ranged from 0.183 to 0.525 between judge pairs with non-overlapping intervals. The serious-or-worse harm-severity rate differed 17.1-fold across judges (0.23%, 2.34% and 3.94%). Requiring two of three judges reduced HIGH+ classification from 13.79% to 2.89%, and no answer met CRITICAL by consensus (0/1,421). FACTFULNESS-target families were more often consensus-inaccurate than non-target families (36.8% vs 27.9%, P=0.002), whereas the COMPLETENESS check was null once refusal-driven security items were excluded (1.7% vs 4.3%, P=0.27). On rescoring byte-identical answers, mean within-judge AC1 was 0.703 against 0.265 between judges, and the consensus risk band was reproduced across all five replicates for 52.0% of items.

 CONCLUSIONS

Treated as a measurement instrument, the battery's reliability and severity grading depended strongly on judge identity and on the task being judged, and one of two planned construct checks behaved as intended. Consensus reduced extreme classifications, and aggregate estimates were reproducible enough to support period-on-period monitoring, whereas single-run item-level verdicts were not. Multi-model batteries are therefore usable for monitoring when consensus is reported with judge-specific dispersion, missingness and stratified reliability. Human-anchored calibration remains necessary before severity scale or risk labels can be interpreted as absolute clinical risk.

 CLINICALTRIAL

NA

title: Evaluating Large Language Models in Turkish Short Answer Scoring: Validity, Reliability, and Fairness Perspectives
abstract: <jats:p xml:lang="en">This study examines the performance of large language models (LLMs) in Turkish short-answer assessments within the measurement and evaluation theory framework. The GPT, Gemini, Gemma, and LLaMA models were evaluated under zero-shot and one-shot conditions with rubric support. The results show that LLMs have high internal consistency, but decision reliability can vary depending on prompt format and example sensitivity. Formulating rubrics with clear and concrete performance indicators increases model-human alignment and assessment fairness. Furthermore, error direction analyses revealed that models can exhibit systematic low-scoring tendencies. The results indicate that LLMs can support teachers in formative assessment with properly structured rubrics, but ethical oversight and pedagogical responsibility remain indispensable in final decisions.</jats:p>

title: Validity, Reliability and Fairness Evidence for the JD-Next Exam
abstract: At a time when institutions of higher education are exploring alternatives to traditional admissionstesting, institutions are also seeking to better support students and prepare them for academicsuccess. Under such an engaged model, one may seek to measure not just the accumulatedknowledge and skills that students would bring to a new academic program, but also their ability togrow and learn through the academic program. To help prepare students for law school before theymatriculate, the JD-Next is a fully-online, non-credit, 7-10 week course to train potential juris doctor(JD) students in case reading and analysis skills. This study builds upon the work presented forprevious JD-Next cohorts by introducing new scoring and reliability estimation methodologies basedon a recent redesign of the assessment for the 2021 cohort, as well as presenting updated validity andfairness findings, using first-year grades, rather than merely first-semester grades as in prior cohorts.Results support the claim that the JD-Next exam is reliable and valid for predicting law schoolsuccess, providing a statistically significant increase in predictive power over baseline modelsincluding entrance exam scores and grade-point average. In terms of fairness across racial and ethnicgroups, smaller score disparities are found with JD-Next than with traditional admissionsassessments, and the assessment is shown to be equally predictive for students from underrepresentedminority groups and first-generation students. These findings, in conjunction with those fromprevious research, support the use of the JD-Next exam for both preparation and admissions offuture law school students.

title: Structural Simulation Benchmark for Reasoning Large Language Models: Accuracy, Reliability, and Failure Modes
abstract: <jats:p>Large language models (LLMs), particularly reasoning-oriented models optimized for long-horizon and multi-step inference, are increasingly used to assist programming and scientific research. However, their reliability in structural engineering computations—where validity is highly sensitive to implementation details—remains insufficiently quantified. This study evaluates four recent reasoning-oriented LLMs (Claude Sonnet 4.5, DeepSeekV3.2, GPT5, and Grok 4 Fastreasoning) under a unified API-based setup with default parameters and proposes a novel evaluation framework tailored for structural simulation. Five problems are designed to cover linear elasticity problems, forced vibration of a Timoshenko beam, and frame analysis. Solution strategies are constrained for comparability, and all generated codes are executed in a fixed Python environment with results verified against ABAQUS simulations or analytical solutions. The framework explicitly probes the importance of boundary conditions, selection of modeling assumptions, and implementation robustness. Common failure modes include incorrect treatment of traction-free boundaries, local-to-global transformation errors due to inconsistent local-axis definitions, and numerical instability induced by the choices of ways to impose boundary conditions. Overall reliability shows GPT‐5 is best model among those models tested. These findings suggest that verification-oriented workflows and automated consistency checks are essential for the safe use of LLM-assisted structural computation.</jats:p>

title: BEYOND MODEL SCALE: A TASK-AWARE RELIABILITY BENCHMARK FOR LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS IN CLINICAL DECISION SUPPORT
abstract: <jats:p>Model size is often treated as a proxy for trustworthiness when large language models (LLMs) are considered for clinical decision support, yet a single aggregate score can hide task-specific failure modes. This paper introduces TARB-CDS, a task-aware reliability audit that transforms a model-by-task accuracy matrix into deployment-relevant reliability profiles. The framework combines macro accuracy with lower-tail conditional value at risk over the two weakest tasks (CVaR-2), worst-task accuracy, Pareto dominance, policy-weighted scores, contextual rank stability under uncertain task mixtures, output-format reliability, and matched base-versus-instruction-tuned comparisons. We conduct a reproducible secondary analysis of 12 LLM checkpoints evaluated on seven Med-HALT reasoning and biomedical-memory tasks. The public reasoning files contain 39,590 rows across False Confidence, Fake Question, and None-of-the-Above tests; published model accuracies and format-error rates are analyzed without claiming fresh model inference. Falcon-40B has the highest seven-task macro accuracy (42.67%) and CVaR-2 (9.36%), but the best worst-task accuracy among all models is only 1.38%. Under 100,000 uniformly sampled task mixtures, Falcon-40B ranks first in 77.60% of contexts, leaving substantial rank instability. Among open checkpoints, parameter count has only a modest descriptive association with macro accuracy (Spearman ρ=0.366), while all five matched instruction/chat-tuning pairs reduce macro accuracy by an average of 9.30 percentage points. These results show that scale alone is insufficient for reliability claims and motivate task-conditional model cards and minimum-performance gates before clinical evaluation.</jats:p>

title: Automated Grading and Professional Accounting Education: Examining the Fairness, Reliability, and Validity of AI Grades
abstract: <jats:p>Automated long-essay scoring (ALES) is gradually considered as a means to enhance efficiency and consistency in large-scale assessment; however, concerns remain regarding its suitability, particularly as it relates to the reliability, validity, and fairness of ALES-assigned grades relative to human-grades in high-stakes professional contexts. This study examines these concerns using over 15,000 long essay examination scripts from a professional accounting certification examination. The study examines whether the ALES confidence index (CI) meaningfully predicts grading accuracy or points to systemic grading failures. Findings reveal fair overall agreement between human and ALES grades, with high within ±1 grade agreement, and rare yet task-concentrated ALES grading failures, while CI shows statistically significant but practically weak predictive value and limited discrimination. The results support the use of ALES as an assistive, human oversight tool rather than an independent grader, highlighting the importance of task-based validation, stronger calibration analysis, and continuous human supervision in high-stakes professional assessment contexts. The study advances innovative assessment practices, but calls for cautious deployment of ALES and recommends integration of a hybrid human-in-the-loop approach, multi-disciplinary validation, and capacity building to strengthen ethical and responsible AI usage in accounting education and professional practice, aligning with SDGs 4 and 9.</jats:p>

title: The Validity and Reliability of the Intercultural Learning Materials Model (ILM) for Drama Subject
abstract: <jats:p>The lecturers still seem unconfidence to teach English as Foreign Language. They need the learning material to reveal the gap between English and the student’s own culture. This study aims to find out the validity and reliability of the intercultural learning material for Drama subject. The research design was quantitative research. The instrumentation of this research was the questionnaire. The subject of this research was 29 students. The results showed that the validity of the ILM model was 92,5 %. It means that the ILM model is valid to use for Drama subject. Then, reliability of intercultural learning materials was 0.774; the ILM model is reliable to use for Drama subject. Based on this result, the intercultural learning materials can implemented because they were categorized as valid and reliable. Thus, the learning materials will be an alternative to link between English and Malay cultures in the lesson process and drama performances.</jats:p>

title: Language-model-derived training data for polymer glass transition prediction: a controlled benchmark
abstract: <jats:p>Experimental glass transition temperatures (Tg) are known for only a few thousand polymers, and each new one costs a synthesis and a measurement. Large language models (LLMs) have read much of the polymer literature and answer questions about polymers for a fraction of a cent. We tested whether such answers can replace or supplement measurements for Tg prediction by two routes: asking Claude Sonnet 5 to write polymers together with their Tg, and asking it to assign a Tg to existing hypothetical polymers. Both datasets were used to train a chemical language model, which was compared on held-out measurements with the same model trained on a growing number of real measurements, alone or after a first stage on the synthetic data. Controls with shuffled Tg values and with the model’s own pseudo-labels separated the value of the LLM’s labels from that of merely seeing more structures. Models trained only on LLM data were about as accurate as the LLM itself and clearly worse than models trained on real data. The LLM data helped only when a few hundred measurements were available, and the benefit disappeared when the Tg values were shuffled. Many “generated” polymers were recalled copies of known polymers, and the LLM’s Tg values were coarse and biased low. LLM-produced data are thus an inexpensive supplement when measurements are scarce, not a substitute for them.</jats:p>

title: FLEX: A Benchmark for Evaluating Robustness of Fairness in Large Language Models
Examining the reliability and validity of bilingual language use and switching measures
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Bilinguals vary in their daily-life language use and switching behaviours, which are also frequently studied in relation to other processes (e.g., executive control). Measuring daily-life language use and switching often relies on self-reported questionnaires, but little is known about the validity of these questionnaires. Here, we present two studies examining test–retest reliability and validity of language-use questionnaires (relative to Ecological Momentary Assessment, Study 1) and language-switching questionnaires and tasks (relative to recorded daily-life conversations, small-scale Study 2). Test–retest reliability and validity of the LSBQ (Anderson et al., 2018) were high and moderate, respectively, suggesting this questionnaire can capture daily-life language use well. Although only examined with a small sample size, Study 2 suggested relatively low validity of most language-switching questionnaires, with short language-production tasks potentially offering a more valid assessment. Together, these studies suggest that tools are available to reliably capture language use and switching with (a certain degree of) validity.</jats:p>

title: EntKGBench: A Benchmark for Evaluating Large Language Model Reasoning on Real-World Enterprise Knowledge Graphs
abstract: <jats:p>Current benchmarks for evaluating graph reasoning in Large Language Models (LLMs) predominantly utilize pre-constructed, idealized graphs, thereby omitting the structural complexity inherent in enterprise environments. To bridge this gap, we introduce EntKGBench (Enterprise Knowledge Graph Benchmark), an evaluation framework constructed from authentic enterprise records spanning Basic Graph Queries to Complex Algorithms to assess query-conditioned graph construction and multi-step reasoning. Our empirical analysis reveals a ``Cold Start&apos;&apos; Penalty: while frontier models perform adequately in zero-shot semantic retrieval, their performance drops significantly when required to extract relevant topological structures from noisy data to execute systematic algorithmic reasoning. Finally, we identify an ``Alignment Tax&apos;&apos; in Reinforcement Learning (RL) applied to graph reasoning: while outcome-based RL enhances target-driven local search, it concurrently degrades stability in sequential reasoning tasks reliant on global context.</jats:p>

Natural Language Processing and Generative AI in the Automated Scoring and Feedback of Reflective Writing in Medical Education: A Validity and Fairness Analysis
abstract: The study explored the application of Natural Language Processing (NLP) and generative AI tools in assessing reflective writing submitted by medical students in Ghana. It evaluated the validity, fairness, and cultural alignment of AI-generated feedback by comparing AI-generated scores with human rater assessments and analyzing demographic group discrepancies. A total of 180 reflective essays were sampled, with an equal number (n = 60) collected from each university. Quantitative methods included Cohen’s Kappa and Intraclass Correlation Coefficients (ICC) to assess inter-rater agreement, while logistic regression and multiple regression models examined potential biases across gender, university affiliation, and English proficiency. Qualitative data were gathered through interviews with students and faculty to explore perceptions of fairness, trust, and the AI’s capacity to capture cultural and linguistic nuances. Results indicated that the AI system demonstrated strong inter-rater reliability, with Cohen’s Kappa values of 0.74 (AI vs Rater 1) and 0.76 (AI vs Rater 2), and ICC values of 0.78 and 0.80, respectively. Human raters showed higher agreement with each other (Cohen’s Kappa = 0.81, ICC = 0.85). However, significant discrepancies were found across demographic groups, particularly for English proficiency, where lower proficiency students tended to receive higher AI scores than human raters (log-odds of 0.45, p = 0.001). Thematic analysis of qualitative interviews revealed concerns over the lack of empathy in AI feedback, misalignment with cultural and linguistic nuances, and mixed levels of trust in AI-generated assessments. These findings suggest that while AI holds promise for improving efficiency in assessment, careful attention must be given to its limitations in fairness and cultural sensitivity. The study concluded with recommendations for improving AI systems through contextual adaptation, hybrid assessment models, faculty training, and regular bias audits to ensure equitable and effective use of AI in educational settings.

title: A validity-guided workflow for robust large language model research in psychology
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are rapidly being integrated into psychological and behavioral research as research tools, evaluation targets, human simulators, and cognitive models. Yet recent evidence reveals severe measurement unreliability: personality assessments degenerate under factor analysis, moral preferences reverse with punctuation changes, and theory-of-mind accuracy varies widely with trivial rephrasing. These “measurement phantoms”—statistical artifacts masquerading as psychological phenomena—threaten the validity of a growing body of research. Guided by the dual-validity framework that integrates psychometrics with causal inference, we present a six-stage workflow that scales validity requirements to research ambition—using LLMs to code text requires basic reliability and accuracy, whereas claims about psychological properties demand comprehensive construct validation. Researchers must (1) explicitly define their research goal and corresponding validity requirements, (2) develop and validate computational instruments through psychometric testing, (3) design experiments that control for computational confounds, (4) execute protocols transparently, (5) analyze data with methods appropriate for non-independent observations, and (6) report findings within boundaries and use results to refine theory. We illustrate the workflow through an example of model evaluation—“LLM selfhood”—showing how systematic validation can distinguish genuine computational phenomena from measurement artifacts. By establishing validated computational instruments and transparent practices, this workflow provides a path toward building a robust empirical foundation for AI psychology research.

title: A Multi-Model, Multi-Domain Benchmark of Large Language Model Agreement with Humans and with Each Other in Sentiment Classification
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used to classify sentiment, yet cross-provider comparisons on the same data are rare and inter-model agreement is largely unmeasured. We evaluate five LLMs from four providers (Claude Opus 4.7, GPT-4o, GPT-5.5, Llama 3.1 8B, and Gemini 2.5 Pro), with VADER (a rule-based lexicon) and RoBERTa (a supervised transformer) as a baseline, on five human-annotated datasets (8,872 sentences) spanning formal and informal text in financial and general domains, under one fixed zero-shot prompt. We report Macro F1 and Cohen’s kappa against human labels, agreement between every model pair, and consensus rates. Claude Opus 4.7 and GPT-5.5 lead (mean Macro F1 0.775 and 0.776; mean kappa versus humans 0.690 and 0.700) and, with GPT-4o, form a tight cluster (pairwise inter-model kappa 0.74 to 0.89); Llama 3.1 8B, which runs locally, is moderate; Gemini 2.5 Pro, served via the Batch API, scores near chance — and a controlled minimum-thinking-budget rerun rules out ”overthinking” (extended deliberation harming a simple task) as the cause. All six deployed classifiers (the five LLMs and VADER) agree on only 14 to 24 percent of sentences depending on the dataset (highest on formal financial text), so model choice materially changes labels, especially on informal text. We release all predictions, code, and data.

title: From Small to Large: Assessing Medical Reasoning, Benchmark Contamination, and Model Scaling in Language Models​
abstract: <jats:p>Large language models (LLMs) now answer medical exam questions at or above expert level, but it is unclear whether such scores reflect clinical competence, or are instead affected by the format of the questions being asked (e.g., multiple-choice versus open-ended), prior exposure to the benchmarks, and the difficulty of the questions. These benchmarks are also public and widely used online, which may be resulting in LLM memorization. Models may perform better on questions that they have seen before. It is also not evident whether smaller models, which are more locally deployable in HIPAA-compliant hospital settings, have achieved human performance. In this study, we evaluate twelve current models from six leading providers, one smaller and one larger model from each provider, on 2,773 questions from three medical benchmarks (MedQA-USMLE, MedMCQA, and PubMedQA) under standard multiple choice, the same questions with the answer choices withheld, and reconstruction of a hidden question from its choices alone. In the standard multiple-choice setting, the strongest models exceed the human-expert baseline on two of three benchmarks, but the smaller models trail their larger models by 8.2 percentage points and only two of the five pass the human-expert bar on the licensing examination. Withholding the answer choices, however, makes every model struggle: mean accuracy falls from 82.8\% to 51.0\%, and the two largest drops belong to the medically specialised models. On memorization, the strongest models reconstruct one question in four from the answer choices alone, yet accuracy holds on the questions they cannot reconstruct. We further weigh accuracy against inference cost and test whether ensembling several models improves medical question answering.</jats:p>

title: Reliability, Validity and Developmental Sensitivity of the Language Use Inventory (LUI) in the Spanish Context (LUI-Spanish)
Scoring the NIH Stroke Scale from bedside exam transcripts: a synthetic benchmark of a decision model and a large language model
abstract:
<jats:p>Background. Clinicians score the NIH Stroke Scale (NIHSS) at the bedside, often under time pressure, and ambient AI tools that listen to clinical encounters are now entering practice. It is not known whether software can score the NIHSS from the exam conversation itself, rather than extract a score that has already been written in a note.
Methods. We created 112 synthetic code-stroke cases. One hundred were allocated in proportion to real code-stroke presentations, and 12 stress cases tested special scoring rules. For each case, a large language model (Claude Opus 5.5) wrote a reference score form (the answer key) and a speech-to-text-style exam transcript, with main-set transcripts split evenly between a narrated and a telegraphic examiner style. A second model (Claude Fable 5.1), blind to the key, scored every transcript and agreed with the key on 99.2% of items. Each transcript was then scored by Jev, a decision model, and by gpt-6-luna, a general large language model (LLM). The primary outcome was item-level accuracy against the key.
Results. The LLM scored 99.0% of items correctly (95% CI 98.4-99.4) and Jev 94.4% (93.2-95.4; McNemar p < 0.001), with exact totals in 101 and 63 of 112 cases. Jev was faster (median 0.15 vs 5.78 s per exam) and cheaper (USD 0.23 vs 0.67 per 1,000 exams). With telegraphic examiners, accuracy fell from 98.0% to 90.9% for Jev and from 100% to 97.7% for the LLM. In a post-hoc analysis that kept only the examiner's words, accuracy stayed high when the examiner narrated (Jev 96.9%, LLM 98.8%) but dropped to about 80% when the examiner used shorthand. Most of Jev's errors fell on four items (language, extinction and neglect, LOC questions and visual fields), and on each it tended to repeat the same mistake, for example scoring slurred speech as aphasia. Its confidence flagged most of these errors. Re-checking the 14.8% of items with confidence below 0.70 would have caught 86% of them, and a simulated hybrid reached 98.8% accuracy.
Conclusions. Both engines scored most NIHSS items correctly from exam transcripts. The LLM was more accurate, and the decision model was faster and cheaper, with a confidence signal that could route uncertain items to an LLM. Because the cases and the key are synthetic, these findings need confirmation with recorded exams and human raters.</jats:p>

title: The Uneven Frontier: User Heterogeneity and the External Validity of Language Model Benchmarks
abstract: <jats:p>Benchmarks treat language model quality as a property of the model. But what users actually experience is jointly produced by the model and the user; and users differ enormously in how skillfully they prompt, evaluate outputs, and choose which problems to bring to AI in the first place. This paper develops a framework for what follows from that fact. We define the quality surface: a landscape over input space whose peaks and valleys are established by the prompt-sensitivity literature. Users navigate this surface with skill-dependent strategies, producing an elicitation divergence. Experienced quality diverges across the population over time, even when everyone uses the same model. We prove that this divergence causes benchmark rankings to lose their predictive power for population outcomes, with rank reversal between models emerging as a special case under empirically realistic conditions. Our framework also reconciles a puzzle in the AI productivity literature: short, constrained tasks compress the productivity distribution and help low-skill workers most, while long, open-ended deployments with task-selection discretion let high-skill workers pull ahead. Both patterns fall out of the same dynamics under different parameters. We propose an elicitability index that measures how much a model's quality depends on user skill, separating forces that reduce this dependence (RLHF, instruction tuning) from forces that amplify it (capability growth, agentic mediation). We establish these results formally and illustrate them through simulations, and we outline an empirical validation strategy using public conversation corpora. The framework names what we call elicitation inequality: users with identical access to the same model can experience it as qualitatively different technologies, depending on how they navigate it. This is a new and currently unmeasured dimension of digital inequality, and it changes what evaluation has to measure, what deployment has to account for, and what governance has to address.</jats:p>

title: Validity of Large Language Model Comparative Judgment for Universal Writing Screening
abstract: Universal writing screening requires scoring approaches that are feasible and supported by validity evidence. This study evaluated large language model (LLM)-based comparative judgment (CJ) for scoring informational writing assessments completed by 1,208 students in Grades 3–6 across three screening occasions. Seven LLMs representing different capability and cost tiers performed pairwise comparisons of writing quality. LLM-based CJ scores showed meaningful convergence with researcher analytic rubric scores (r = .59–.73). For single-wave scores, LLM-based CJ was comparable to researcher scoring in predicting state writing rubric scores and generally matched or exceeded it in predicting ELA scale scores and classifying ELA proficiency. Averaging scores across three screening waves substantially improved criterion-related validity and classification accuracy, with LLM-based CJ reaching β = .59–.66 for state writing rubric scores, β = .68–.74 for ELA scale scores, and AUC = .82–.86 for ELA proficiency. Predictive bias patterns for multilingual learners were similar across scoring methods. Findings were broadly consistent across LLMs, with little evidence that greater model capability or cost improved validity evidence. Results support LLM-based CJ as a promising approach for efficient writing screening and highlight the value of multiple writing samples per student and task-specific evaluation of validity relative to cost.

title: Validity, Reliability, and Fairness Evidence for the <scp>JD‐Next</scp> Exam
abstract: <jats:p>At a time when institutions of higher education are exploring alternatives to traditional admissions testing, institutions are also seeking to better support students and prepare them for academic success. Under such an engaged model, one may seek to measure not just the accumulated knowledge and skills that students would bring to a new academic program but also their ability to grow and learn through the academic program. To help prepare students for law school before they matriculate, the JD‐Next is a fully online, noncredit, 7‐ to 10‐week course to train potential juris doctor students in case reading and analysis skills. This study builds on the work presented for previous JD‐Next cohorts by introducing new scoring and reliability estimation methodologies based on a recent redesign of the assessment for the 2021 cohort, and it presents updated validity and fairness findings using first‐year grades, rather than merely first‐semester grades as in prior cohorts. Results support the claim that the JD‐Next exam is reliable and valid for predicting law school success, providing a statistically significant increase in predictive power over baseline models, including entrance exam scores and grade point averages. In terms of fairness across racial and ethnic groups, smaller score disparities are found with JD‐Next than with traditional admissions assessments, and the assessment is shown to be equally predictive for students from underrepresented minority groups and for first‐generation students. These findings, in conjunction with those from previous research, support the use of the JD‐Next exam for both preparing and admitting future law school students.</jats:p>

title: The Validity and Reliability Grade Primary School EFL Students’ Final Speaking Test
abstract: <jats:p>The study underscores the essential importance of mastering English speaking skills at an early age as mandated by Indonesia’s Merdeka curriculum, which establishes English speaking as a vital subject for assessment in primary education. To ensure the effectiveness of the speaking test used for sixth-grade EFL students, the study focuses on evaluating the validity and reliability of the test. Using a qualitative methodology that combines interviews with an English teacher serving as the rater and document analysis, the research investigates multiple facets of test quality. The findings demonstrate that the speaking test is valid through the application of content validity—confirming the relevance and representativeness of test items—and consequential validity, which considers the implications and fairness of the test outcomes. Moreover, reliability is verified via intra-rater reliability, indicating that the scoring is consistent when conducted by the same evaluator over time. Ultimately, the study concludes that the speaking test for sixth-grade primary school EFL students possesses excellent quality in both validity and reliability. Consequently, it suggests that other educational institutions with similar levels and objectives may confidently adopt or adapt the test’s design, scoring rubric, and rating procedures to improve their own assessment practices</jats:p>
